sections.title: Preface
sections.html:
Preface

Property and casualty insurance feels difficult at first because the examination uses ordinary words with precise contractual meanings. Collision, vacancy, occurrence, property damage, and insured may mean something narrower than they mean in daily conversation. Once those definitions are organized, the subject becomes a series of repeatable decisions: identify the risk, locate the coverage grant, test the exclusions, apply the conditions, and calculate the amount.

This book teaches that decision process. It begins with the ideas common to every policy, moves through personal and commercial forms, and finishes with the Texas law that governs insurers and producers. The examples explain why a rule works. The review questions then ask you to recognize the rule in a new situation.

Use this manuscript as both a learning book and a reference. Highlight distinctions, complete calculations on paper, and keep a list of missed concepts. Your goal is not to memorize paragraphs. Your goal is to choose the right rule when four answers compete for your attention.

Chapter 1 How to Use This Book and Understand the Texas Exam

Learning Objectives

Understand the two-part exam and its weighting

Build a study schedule around the official outline

Use scenario questions without memorizing isolated words

The examination you are preparing for

The Texas General Lines Property and Casualty examination tests two bodies of knowledge. The national or general portion covers insurance concepts and standard personal and commercial policy forms. The state portion tests Texas statutes, rules, market mechanisms, and producer responsibilities. The official outline effective September 1, 2026 lists 100 scoreable general questions and 30 scoreable Texas questions. It also lists 10 general and 5 state pretest questions that do not affect the score. Because pretest questions are mixed into the examination and are not identified, answer every question as if it counts.

Pearson VUE currently lists 150 minutes for the English General Lines Property and Casualty examination and a $49 examination fee. The reported passing standard is a scaled score of 70. A scaled score is not the percentage of questions answered correctly. Different examination forms are equated for difficulty, so the raw number needed to pass can vary. Always verify scheduling details and fees before registering.

What receives the most attention

The general outline assigns 22 questions to property policy types, 23 to casualty policies and related terms, 15 to general insurance concepts, 15 to casualty concepts, 13 to property contract provisions, and 12 to casualty policy provisions. The Texas outline assigns 18 questions to laws common to property and casualty insurance and 12 to Texas rules unique to P&C. This distribution tells you how to study: policy comparisons, liability concepts, and Texas producer law deserve repeated review.

Do not study homeowners and auto alone. The General Lines license includes commercial property, commercial general liability, business auto, workers compensation, crime, bonds, professional liability, umbrella coverage, and business owners policies. Commercial lines account for a large part of the outline.

A four week study plan

Week one should cover fundamentals, contracts, valuation, negligence, dwelling, and homeowners. Week two should cover personal auto, commercial property, business income, BOP, and CGL. Week three should cover business auto, workers compensation, crime, bonds, professional liability, flood, and special property. Week four should focus on Texas law, timed practice, error review, and formulas.

Use active recall. Close the book and explain a concept in your own words. Compare similar forms in a small chart. For every missed question, write why the correct answer is right and why your choice was wrong. Retake a question only after you can state the rule without seeing the options.

A method for scenario questions

Read the final sentence first so you know what the question asks. Identify the policy, coverage part, cause of loss, insured, property, location, timing, and applicable exclusion. Then apply the rule. Words such as always, never, only, and automatically often make an option too broad. When two answers look plausible, choose the one that states the more precise policy rule.

This book uses standard industry forms and exam conventions. An actual insurer may modify a form with endorsements. For the examination, follow the form and facts presented in the question. Do not add facts from personal experience.

Memory Rule General knowledge 100 scored plus 10 pretest. Texas law 30 scored plus 5 pretest. Total time 150 minutes. Passing score 70 scaled.

Chapter Review

1. Which statement best describes pure risk?

A. It offers loss or gain

B. It offers loss or no loss

C. It always produces loss

D. It cannot be transferred

2. Faulty electrical wiring is which type of hazard?

A. Moral

B. Morale

C. Physical

D. Legal

3. An insured intentionally exaggerates stolen property. This is primarily a

A. Physical hazard

B. Moral hazard

C. Morale hazard

D. Speculative risk

Answers

1. B. Pure risk has the possibility of loss or no loss and is generally the type insurance addresses.

2. C. Faulty wiring is a tangible condition that increases the chance of fire.

3. B. Dishonest intent is a moral hazard.

sections.title: Chapter 2  Risk Insurance and the Law of Large Numbers
sections.html:
Chapter 2 Risk Insurance and the Law of Large Numbers

Learning Objectives

Separate pure risk from speculative risk

Recognize perils and the three hazard categories

Apply risk management methods and insurable risk characteristics

Risk and uncertainty

Risk is uncertainty concerning a loss. Pure risk offers the possibility of loss or no loss and is generally insurable. A house may burn or remain intact. Speculative risk offers a possibility of loss, no loss, or gain. Buying stock or opening a business is speculative and ordinarily is not insured as such.

Insurance transfers the financial consequences of covered pure risks from the insured to the insurer in exchange for premium. It does not prevent the event. The principle of indemnity seeks to restore an insured approximately to the financial position occupied before the loss, subject to policy limits, deductibles, valuation clauses, and other terms.

Peril exposure and hazard

A peril is the direct cause of loss, such as fire, wind, theft, or collision. A hazard is a condition that increases the chance or severity of loss. A physical hazard is tangible, such as faulty wiring. A moral hazard arises from dishonesty or an incentive to cause or exaggerate a loss. A morale hazard arises from carelessness or indifference because insurance exists. Leaving keys in an unlocked car is usually a morale hazard; deliberately arranging a theft is a moral hazard.

An exposure is a person, property, activity, or condition that could produce loss. A frame building, a delivery fleet, and a store that admits customers all create exposures. Underwriting evaluates exposures and hazards to decide whether to insure and at what price and terms.

The law of large numbers

The law of large numbers allows an insurer to predict group losses more reliably as it observes more similar, independent exposure units. It does not predict which particular house will burn. Pooling many exposure units makes actual results more likely to approach expected results.

An ideally insurable risk involves many similar exposure units, accidental and measurable loss, a determinable time and place, affordable premium, and a loss that is not catastrophic to the entire pool. Insurers manage catastrophic accumulation through underwriting, geographic spread, reinsurance, deductibles, exclusions, and specialized markets.

Risk management methods

Avoidance eliminates an activity, as when a company stops making a dangerous product. Retention means the person or business pays some or all loss, deliberately or unintentionally. A deductible is planned retention. Reduction lowers frequency or severity through sprinklers, alarms, training, or loss-control programs. Transfer shifts financial consequences by insurance or contract. Sharing distributes loss among participants.

The examination often gives an action and asks for the method. Focus on what the action does. Installing a sprinkler is reduction, purchasing insurance is transfer, and choosing not to own a swimming pool is avoidance.

Memory Rule Peril causes loss. Hazard increases loss. Pure risk is insurable; speculative risk includes gain. Avoid, retain, reduce, transfer, or share.

Chapter Review

1. The law of large numbers helps an insurer

A. Predict exactly who will have a loss

B. Eliminate catastrophic loss

C. Predict aggregate losses more reliably

D. Insure speculative gains

2. Which is consideration from an applicant?

A. Only the insurer promise

B. Premium and statements in the application

C. The declarations

D. The deductible alone

3. An insurance policy is aleatory because

A. Only one party makes a promise

B. It is drafted by one party

C. Values exchanged may be unequal and depend on chance

D. It must be in writing

Answers

1. C. More similar exposure units improve the reliability of aggregate loss predictions.

2. B. The applicant consideration includes premium and application representations.

3. C. An uncertain event determines whether and how much the insurer pays.

sections.title: Chapter 3  Insurance Contracts and Policy Structure
sections.html:
Chapter 3 Insurance Contracts and Policy Structure

Learning Objectives

Identify the four elements of a valid contract

Explain adhesion aleatory unilateral and conditional

Navigate declarations insuring agreements exclusions and conditions

Elements of a valid contract

A valid contract requires competent parties, legal purpose, offer and acceptance, and consideration. The applicant normally makes an offer by submitting an application and premium. The insurer accepts by issuing coverage as requested or may make a counteroffer by changing terms. The applicant gives statements and premium as consideration; the insurer gives its promise to pay covered claims.

A binder is temporary evidence of insurance pending policy issuance. It generally contains essential terms such as parties, property or risk, coverage, limits, effective time, and duration. A binder does not create coverage the insurer is legally unable to provide, and it ends according to its terms or when replaced by the policy.

Special characteristics

Insurance is a contract of adhesion because the insurer drafts the form and the insured usually accepts it as written. Courts generally interpret genuine ambiguity against the drafter. It is aleatory because values exchanged may be unequal and depend on an uncertain event. It is unilateral because only the insurer makes a legally enforceable promise to pay once the insured performs required conditions. It is conditional because obligations depend on compliance with policy conditions.

Property insurance is also personal: it protects the insured financial interest rather than guaranteeing the property itself. Assignment of a policy before loss generally requires the insurer consent because the insured risk could change. Assignment of claim proceeds after a loss is different because the loss has already fixed the obligation.

Parts of a policy

Declarations personalize the contract by naming the insured, policy period, property or operations, limits, deductibles, forms, and premium. The insuring agreement states the insurer basic promise. Definitions give special meanings to important words. Exclusions remove specified causes, property, persons, or circumstances. Conditions state duties and rules that affect coverage. Endorsements add, remove, or modify provisions and control over conflicting preprinted language.

Always read a coverage question in this order: Is the person or property insured? Did a covered cause of loss occur during the policy period and territory? Does an exclusion apply? Does an exception restore coverage? Were conditions satisfied? What limit, deductible, and valuation method govern the amount?

Representations concealment and warranties

A representation is a statement believed true to the best of the applicant knowledge. A material misrepresentation can affect underwriting and may permit rescission or other remedies allowed by law. Concealment is the failure to disclose a material fact. Fraud adds intent to deceive. A warranty is a statement or promise guaranteed to be true and is treated more strictly than an ordinary representation.

Insurance applicants and insurers owe good faith in the transaction. Producers must submit complete and accurate applications, avoid altering answers without authorization, and explain that final coverage depends on the insurer and policy terms.

Memory Rule Contract elements are competent parties legal purpose offer and acceptance and consideration. Policy order is declarations insuring agreement definitions exclusions conditions endorsements.

Chapter Review

1. An endorsement conflicts with a preprinted policy provision. Which generally controls?

A. The application

B. The endorsement

C. The older wording

D. The producer notes

2. Temporary evidence of coverage pending policy issuance is a

A. Certificate

B. Binder

C. Warranty

D. Proof of loss

3. Replacement cost is $30,000 and depreciation is $9,000. ACV is

A. $9,000

B. $21,000

C. $30,000

D. $39,000

Answers

1. B. An endorsement modifies the contract and controls over conflicting standard wording.

2. B. A binder provides temporary insurance subject to its terms.

3. B. ACV is commonly calculated as replacement cost minus depreciation: $30,000 minus $9,000.

sections.title: Chapter 4  Property Loss Valuation Deductibles and Coinsurance
sections.html:
Chapter 4 Property Loss Valuation Deductibles and Coinsurance

Learning Objectives

Calculate actual cash value and coinsurance

Distinguish replacement market stated and agreed value

Apply limits deductibles and insurance to value

Valuation methods

Replacement cost is the cost to repair or replace damaged property with new property of like kind and quality without deducting depreciation. Actual cash value is commonly tested as replacement cost minus depreciation. Market value is the price a willing buyer would pay a willing seller and can differ greatly from construction cost. Agreed value suspends or replaces a coinsurance requirement when the insurer and insured agree on value. Stated value establishes an amount shown in the policy but may still allow payment of the lesser of stated amount, actual cash value, or repair cost depending on the form. Functional replacement cost uses less costly materials or methods that perform the same function.

Salvage value is the value remaining in damaged property. When an insurer pays a total loss and takes salvage, the insured cannot also keep the salvage value without adjustment because that could exceed indemnity.

Deductibles and limits

A deductible is the amount the insured absorbs before the insurer pays. A higher deductible normally lowers premium and reduces small claims. A per-occurrence deductible applies to each occurrence. An aggregate deductible accumulates covered losses during a period before coverage begins. A franchise deductible pays nothing below a threshold but may pay the full loss once the threshold is reached.

A specific limit applies to one item or location. A blanket limit applies across more than one item, type, or location. Sublimits cap particular property or causes of loss within the overall limit. Policy limits are ceilings, not automatic payments.

Coinsurance formula

Commercial property coinsurance encourages insurance to value. The standard exam formula is: amount carried divided by amount required, multiplied by the covered loss, minus the deductible. The amount required equals the property value at the time of loss multiplied by the coinsurance percentage.

Example: A building has a value of $500,000 and an 80 percent coinsurance requirement. Required insurance is $400,000. The insured carries $300,000 and has a $100,000 covered loss with a $1,000 deductible. The ratio is $300,000 divided by $400,000, or 0.75. The insurer calculation is 0.75 times $100,000, less $1,000, producing $74,000, subject to all policy terms. Compare that result with the policy limit and never pay more than the loss.

Proximate cause and concurrent events

Proximate cause is the dominant cause that sets an unbroken chain of events in motion. The immediate event is not always the proximate cause. If lightning causes a fire and water used to extinguish the fire damages property, the covered lightning or fire event may be the proximate cause of the resulting damage.

Named-peril coverage requires the insured to show that a listed peril caused the loss. Open-peril coverage generally covers direct physical loss unless excluded, after which an exclusion and any exception must be analyzed. Open peril does not mean every loss is covered.

Memory Rule ACV equals replacement cost minus depreciation. Coinsurance payment equals carried divided by required times loss minus deductible.

Chapter Review

1. A building worth $400,000 has an 80 percent coinsurance clause. Required insurance is

A. $80,000

B. $320,000

C. $400,000

D. $480,000

2. Which is normally deducted after the coinsurance calculation?

A. Premium

B. Salvage

C. Deductible

D. Market value

3. The dominant cause that starts an unbroken chain of events is

A. Appraisal

B. Proximate cause

C. Indemnity

D. Subrogation

Answers

1. B. $400,000 multiplied by 80 percent equals $320,000.

2. C. The exam formula applies the coinsurance ratio to the loss and then subtracts the deductible.

3. B. Proximate cause is the dominant cause producing the loss sequence.

sections.title: Chapter 5  Liability Negligence and Damages
sections.html:
Chapter 5 Liability Negligence and Damages

Learning Objectives

Prove the four elements of negligence

Separate strict absolute and vicarious liability

Recognize bodily injury property damage and damage categories

The negligence framework

Negligence is failure to use the degree of care a reasonably prudent person would use under similar circumstances. A claimant generally must establish duty, breach of duty, actual injury or damage, and causation. Causation includes a factual connection and proximate cause. If any required element is missing, negligence is not established.

An intervening event may break the causal chain if it is sufficiently independent and unforeseeable. Defenses can include comparative negligence, assumption of risk, and statutes of limitation, but examination questions usually focus first on the four basic elements.

Types of liability

Vicarious liability places responsibility on one party for another party conduct because of a relationship, such as an employer for an employee acting within the scope of employment. Strict liability may apply without proof of negligence to certain dangerous activities, defective products, or statutory situations. Absolute liability is an exam term for liability imposed without ordinary defenses in narrowly defined circumstances.

Premises and operations exposure arises from ownership or operation of premises and ongoing work. Products and completed operations exposure arises after a product leaves the insured possession or work is completed. This timing distinction is central to CGL questions.

Damages

Compensatory damages reimburse an injured party. Special damages are measurable economic losses such as medical bills, lost wages, and repair costs. General damages are noneconomic losses such as pain, suffering, or disfigurement. Punitive or exemplary damages punish and deter particularly wrongful conduct and may be restricted by law or policy.

Bodily injury generally means bodily injury, sickness, or disease and may include resulting death. Property damage generally includes physical injury to tangible property and loss of use. Personal and advertising injury covers specified offenses, not bodily injury in the ordinary sense. Examples include false arrest, malicious prosecution, wrongful eviction, certain defamation, and specified advertising offenses.

Occurrence and claims made

An occurrence form generally responds when covered injury or damage occurs during the policy period, even if the claim is reported later, subject to notice and other rules. A claims-made form generally requires the claim to be made during the policy period or extended reporting period and after any retroactive date requirements are satisfied. A retroactive date prevents coverage for acts before that date. An extended reporting period provides additional time to report claims; it does not extend the period in which wrongful acts may occur.

Do not confuse an occurrence limit with the event definition. Per-occurrence limits cap payment for one occurrence. Aggregate limits cap specified payments during the policy period.

Memory Rule Negligence requires duty breach causation and damages. Special damages are measurable. General damages are noneconomic. Punitive damages punish.

Chapter Review

1. An employer liable for an employee negligence within employment illustrates

A. Strict liability

B. Vicarious liability

C. Absolute liability

D. Contractual subrogation

2. Medical bills and lost wages are usually

A. General damages

B. Special damages

C. Punitive damages

D. Nominal premiums

3. Pain and suffering is usually

A. General damages

B. Special damages

C. Property damage

D. Restitution premium

Answers

1. B. Vicarious liability arises from a legally recognized relationship.

2. B. Special damages are measurable economic losses.

3. A. General damages are noneconomic losses.

sections.title: Chapter 6  Underwriting Applications and Claims Duties
sections.html:
Chapter 6 Underwriting Applications and Claims Duties

Learning Objectives

Recognize underwriting information sources

Apply FCRA and privacy principles

Sequence insured and insurer duties after loss

Underwriting and rating

Underwriting selects and classifies risks. The application is a primary source, but insurers may also use inspections, motor vehicle reports, loss histories, credit-based information where permitted, financial information, consumer reports, and producer observations. A rate is the price per unit of exposure; premium is the amount charged after rates and rating factors are applied.

Adverse selection occurs when people with a greater-than-average probability of loss are more likely to seek or retain insurance. Underwriting, classifications, deductibles, exclusions, and pricing help control it. Loss ratio compares incurred losses and loss-adjustment expenses with earned premium. Expense ratio compares underwriting expenses with written or earned premium depending on the convention. The combined ratio is commonly the loss ratio plus expense ratio.

Consumer reports and privacy

The Fair Credit Reporting Act governs consumer reports. When an insurer takes adverse action based wholly or partly on information in a consumer report, it must provide the required notice identifying the reporting agency and the consumer rights. The reporting agency does not make the insurer underwriting decision.

The Gramm Leach Bliley framework requires financial institutions to protect nonpublic personal information and provide applicable privacy notices and choices. Exam questions emphasize authorized use, disclosure, security, and notice rather than technical cybersecurity details.

Duties after a property loss

Common insured duties include giving prompt notice, protecting property from further damage, making reasonable temporary repairs, separating damaged from undamaged property when appropriate, preparing an inventory, showing damaged property, cooperating, submitting to examination under oath when required, and providing a signed proof of loss when requested. The insured should document reasonable expenses and must not abandon property to the insurer.

The insurer investigates, determines coverage, communicates required notices, pays covered claims according to the contract and law, and defends covered liability claims when a duty to defend applies. The duty to defend is generally broader than the duty to indemnify because the allegations may create a potential for coverage.

Appraisal subrogation and other insurance

Appraisal is designed to resolve disputes about the amount of a property loss, not whether the policy covers it. Each party selects an appraiser and the appraisers select an umpire. Agreement by any two usually establishes the amount under standard wording.

Subrogation allows an insurer that paid a loss to pursue a responsible third party to the extent of payment. The insured must preserve those rights. Other-insurance provisions coordinate policies through pro rata, excess, contribution by equal shares, or other stated methods. They help prevent duplicate recovery beyond the loss.

Memory Rule Appraisal decides amount not coverage. Subrogation transfers recovery rights after payment. FCRA adverse action requires notice.

Chapter Review

1. Appraisal usually resolves a dispute about

A. Whether fraud occurred

B. The amount of property loss

C. Producer licensing

D. Legal liability

2. After paying a covered loss, an insurer pursues the responsible third party through

A. Contribution

B. Subrogation

C. Estoppel

D. Waiver

3. An adverse underwriting decision based on a consumer report triggers duties under the

A. FCRA

B. TRIA

C. NFIP

D. CGL

Answers

1. B. Appraisal determines amount, not the coverage question.

2. B. Subrogation transfers recovery rights to the paying insurer to the extent of payment.

3. A. The Fair Credit Reporting Act governs consumer reports and adverse-action notice.

sections.title: Chapter 7  Dwelling Insurance Forms
sections.html:
Chapter 7 Dwelling Insurance Forms

Learning Objectives

Compare DP 1 DP 2 and DP 3

Identify dwelling coverage letters

Apply vacancy theft and loss settlement rules

Purpose and coverage structure

Dwelling policies are often used for non-owner-occupied homes, older properties, seasonal dwellings, or risks that do not fit a homeowners form. Coverage A covers the dwelling; Coverage B covers other structures; Coverage C covers personal property; Coverage D covers fair rental value and, when provided by the form, additional living expense; Coverage E provides personal liability when added; Coverage F provides medical payments to others when added. Liability is not automatically part of the basic dwelling property form.

Dwelling forms do not require the broad package approach of homeowners policies. The insured chooses property coverages and may add liability. Coverage C can cover personal property owned or used by the insured, subject to form restrictions.

The three forms

DP 1 Basic is a named-peril form. Its core perils are fire, lightning, and internal explosion. Extended coverage and vandalism or malicious mischief can be added. Losses are generally settled at actual cash value unless modified. DP 2 Broad is a named-peril form that adds perils such as falling objects, weight of ice snow or sleet, accidental discharge of water or steam, sudden cracking of systems, freezing, and electrical damage. DP 3 Special provides open-peril coverage for the dwelling and other structures while personal property remains named peril.

The examination favors comparisons. DP 3 is not open peril for all property. Coverage C remains named peril. Theft is not automatically included in every dwelling form and commonly requires an endorsement.

Fair rental value and additional living expense

Fair rental value reimburses lost rental income when a covered loss makes rented premises unfit for normal use, less expenses that do not continue. Additional living expense reimburses the necessary increase in living expense that permits the household to maintain its normal standard of living after a covered loss. Neither coverage pays the insured ordinary expenses that would have occurred anyway.

Civil authority coverage may apply for a limited time when a covered neighboring loss causes authorities to prohibit use. The exact form language controls.

Common restrictions

Vacancy and unoccupancy are distinct. A vacant building lacks people and enough contents for normal use. An unoccupied building contains furnishings but no occupants. Standard forms restrict certain losses after a stated vacancy period. Freezing coverage commonly depends on maintaining heat or shutting off the water and draining systems. Vandalism and glass losses may be restricted after extended vacancy.

The insured should insure the dwelling to value. Replacement cost settlement usually depends on form, amount carried, and actual repair or replacement. The exam may require ACV until replacement is completed.

Memory Rule DP 1 is basic named peril. DP 2 is broad named peril. DP 3 is open peril on dwelling and structures but named peril on personal property.

Chapter Review

1. The duty to defend is generally

A. Narrower than indemnity

B. Broader than indemnity

C. Identical to appraisal

D. A property valuation rule

2. Which dwelling form is basic named peril?

A. DP 1

B. DP 2

C. DP 3

D. HO 5

3. Under DP 3, personal property is generally covered on which basis?

A. Open peril

B. Named peril

C. Liability only

D. Agreed value only

Answers

1. B. Potentially covered allegations may trigger defense even when indemnity is ultimately not owed.

2. A. DP 1 is the Basic Form.

3. B. DP 3 gives open-peril protection to the dwelling and structures, while contents remain named peril.

sections.title: Chapter 8  Homeowners Forms and Eligibility
sections.html:
Chapter 8 Homeowners Forms and Eligibility

Learning Objectives

Match HO forms to occupants and buildings

Distinguish open and named peril coverage

Identify Section I and Section II

The homeowners package

A homeowners policy combines property and personal liability coverage. Section I covers property. Section II covers personal liability and medical payments to others. Eligibility generally involves an owner-occupied one- to four-family dwelling, a tenant, or a condominium unit owner depending on the form. Business and farming exposures require separate analysis or endorsements.

The named insured, resident spouse, resident relatives, and certain other residents such as persons under 21 in their care may qualify as insureds under definitions. Definitions vary by form, so read the question carefully.

Form comparison

HO 2 Broad covers the dwelling, other structures, and personal property against named broad perils. HO 3 Special provides open-peril coverage for the dwelling and other structures and named-peril coverage for personal property. HO 4 Contents Broad is designed for tenants and primarily covers personal property, loss of use, and liability; the tenant does not insure the building. HO 5 Comprehensive generally provides open-peril coverage for both dwelling and personal property, subject to exclusions. HO 6 Unit Owners covers condominium unit-owner property interests, personal property, loss of use, loss assessment subject to terms, and liability. HO 8 Modified Coverage is designed for certain older homes where replacement cost may greatly exceed market value and uses more limited coverage and valuation.

Memory order: HO 4 rents; HO 6 owns a unit; HO 8 older home. HO 3 is the common owner form with open-peril building coverage. HO 5 broadens personal property to open peril.

Covered property

Coverage A covers the residence premises dwelling and attached structures. Coverage B covers other structures separated by clear space, such as a detached garage, subject to exclusions and limitations. Coverage C covers personal property owned or used by an insured, with limited coverage for property of others in some circumstances. Coverage D covers loss of use, including additional living expense and fair rental value.

Property commonly excluded or sharply limited includes motor vehicles except narrow exceptions, aircraft, certain watercraft, animals, and property of roomers or tenants unrelated to an insured. Special limits commonly apply to money, securities, watercraft, trailers, theft of jewelry, firearms, silverware, and business property. A scheduled personal property endorsement can broaden protection and increase limits for valuable articles.

Covered perils and exclusions

Named-peril personal property coverage commonly includes fire or lightning, windstorm or hail, explosion, riot, aircraft, vehicles, smoke, vandalism, theft, falling objects, weight of ice snow or sleet, accidental discharge or overflow, sudden cracking, freezing, electrical damage, and volcanic eruption, subject to each peril wording.

Major exclusions include ordinance or law, earth movement, water or flood, power failure originating off premises, neglect, war, nuclear hazard, intentional loss, and governmental action, although endorsements or limited additional coverages can modify some exclusions. Wear, deterioration, mechanical breakdown, rust, mold, insects, and faulty workmanship are commonly excluded as causes but ensuing covered loss may require separate analysis.

Memory Rule HO 2 broad named peril. HO 3 open dwelling named contents. HO 4 tenant. HO 5 open dwelling and contents. HO 6 condo. HO 8 modified older home.

Chapter Review

1. Which coverage is not automatically part of the dwelling property form?

A. Dwelling

B. Other structures

C. Personal liability

D. Personal property

2. A furnished home with no residents is best described as

A. Vacant

B. Unoccupied

C. Abandoned to the insurer

D. A total loss

3. Which homeowners form is designed for tenants?

A. HO 3

B. HO 4

C. HO 5

D. HO 6

Answers

1. C. Liability is added rather than automatically packaged in the basic dwelling form.

2. B. Unoccupied normally means contents remain but people are absent.

3. B. HO 4 is the tenants or contents broad form.

sections.title: Chapter 9  Homeowners Coverages Conditions and Liability
sections.html:
Chapter 9 Homeowners Coverages Conditions and Liability

Learning Objectives

Apply additional coverages and loss settlement

Analyze personal liability and medical payments

Recognize major Section II exclusions

Property settlement

Homeowners dwelling losses are commonly settled at replacement cost when the insured meets insurance-to-value and replacement requirements. Personal property is commonly settled at actual cash value unless replacement cost coverage is added. Trees shrubs and plants, debris removal, reasonable repairs, fire department service charges, property removed, credit-card loss, and loss assessment may receive limited additional coverage under the form.

The mortgage clause protects the mortgagee separate interest. A mortgagee may retain protection despite certain acts of the insured if it meets its own duties, pays premium when required, and notifies the insurer of known changes. When the insurer pays a mortgagee and denies the insured, subrogation or assignment rights may follow.

Coverage E personal liability

Coverage E responds when a claim or suit seeks damages because of bodily injury or property damage caused by an occurrence to which coverage applies. The insurer may defend even a groundless suit, but the defense obligation ends as stated after the applicable limit is exhausted by covered payment. Defense costs are generally supplementary and may be paid in addition to the liability limit under standard wording.

Coverage E is not limited to the residence premises. It can follow the insured worldwide, subject to territory and exclusions. The policy also provides limited coverage for damage to property of others, but it is not a substitute for broad property insurance.

Coverage F medical payments to others

Coverage F pays necessary medical expenses for eligible persons, generally without requiring proof that the insured was negligent. It commonly applies to a person on the insured location with permission and, away from the location, to injury caused by an insured, a residence employee, or an animal owned by or in the care of an insured. It generally does not cover the named insured or regular residents of the household, except residence employees in appropriate circumstances.

Medical payments is designed for smaller injuries and goodwill. Personal liability addresses legal liability and has a much larger limit.

Section II exclusions

Important exclusions involve expected or intended injury, business activities, professional services, motor vehicles, many watercraft and aircraft exposures, war, communicable disease in some forms, controlled substances, and injury to an insured. Exceptions and endorsements matter. A home-based business often needs a business endorsement or commercial policy.

Motor vehicle exclusions contain exceptions for vehicles in dead storage, vehicles used solely to service a residence, certain recreational vehicles, and vehicles designed to assist persons with disabilities. Do not assume every motorized device is excluded without reading the exception.

Memory Rule Coverage E requires legal liability. Coverage F can pay eligible medical expenses without negligence. Homeowners property is Section I and liability is Section II.

Chapter Review

1. HO 3 generally provides open-peril coverage on

A. Personal property only

B. Dwelling and other structures

C. Liability only

D. Jewelry only

2. HO 5 generally differs from HO 3 by providing

A. No liability

B. Open-peril personal property coverage

C. Only tenant coverage

D. Farm liability

3. HO 8 is primarily associated with

A. New commercial buildings

B. Older homes and modified coverage

C. Condominium associations

D. Autos

Answers

1. B. HO 3 is open peril for the dwelling and other structures and named peril for contents.

2. B. HO 5 generally broadens personal property to open peril.

3. B. HO 8 addresses certain older homes where replacement cost may be disproportionate.

sections.title: Chapter 10  Special Residential Property Flood Wind and Inland Marine
sections.html:
Chapter 10 Special Residential Property Flood Wind and Inland Marine

Learning Objectives

Recognize flood and wind gaps

Understand personal inland marine floaters

Select coverage for mobile homes watercraft farm and earthquake

Flood and the NFIP

Standard dwelling and homeowners policies exclude flood. Flood generally involves temporary inundation of normally dry land affecting the required area or number of properties under the governing definition. Surface water, overflow of inland or tidal waters, mudflow, and erosion-related collapse may qualify under program rules; sewer backup alone does not become flood unless directly caused by flood.

The National Flood Insurance Program provides building and contents coverage through participating communities and insurers using federal rules. Building and contents are separate limits and usually have separate deductibles. Coverage ordinarily has a waiting period unless an exception applies, such as certain loan transactions. The program does not duplicate homeowners loss-of-use coverage in the same way. Candidates should verify current NFIP limits and rules because Congress and FEMA may change them.

Windstorm and earthquake

Windstorm is commonly covered under homeowners forms, but coastal policies may exclude wind and hail and require separate windstorm coverage. Texas Windstorm Insurance Association is an insurer of last resort for eligible coastal property that cannot obtain wind and hail coverage in the voluntary market. Eligibility, inspections, certificates, and property standards matter.

Earth movement is excluded under standard homeowners forms. Earthquake coverage can be endorsed or purchased separately. Earthquake deductibles are commonly percentages rather than flat amounts and may apply separately by coverage or event depending on the form.

Inland marine

Inland marine insurance covers movable property, property in transit, instrumentalities of transportation and communication, and specialized property. A personal articles floater schedules valuable items such as jewelry, fine arts, cameras, musical instruments, and collectibles. It commonly offers broad open-peril coverage, agreed or scheduled values, and worldwide territory, subject to exclusions.

Commercial inland marine examples include contractors equipment, installation floaters, accounts receivable, valuable papers, electronic data processing equipment, motor truck cargo, and bailees customers coverage. A bailee temporarily holds property of others for a purpose such as repair, cleaning, or storage.

Other residential forms

A mobilehome endorsement or specialized policy adapts dwelling language to a manufactured or mobile home and its related property. Watercraft coverage under homeowners is limited by size, type, and use; larger or faster boats need a separate policy. Farm insurance combines dwelling, farm personal property, barns and structures, liability, and farming exposures. Personal homeowners forms generally exclude farming conducted as a business.

Ordinance or law coverage addresses increased rebuilding cost caused by enforcement of building codes. Service line, equipment breakdown, water backup, identity fraud, and home-business endorsements cover distinct gaps and should not be confused with ordinary wear and tear.

Memory Rule Homeowners excludes flood and earth movement. Inland marine follows movable or specialized property. TWIA addresses eligible coastal wind and hail.

Chapter Review

1. Homeowners Coverage D is

A. Dwelling

B. Other structures

C. Loss of use

D. Personal liability

2. Homeowners Coverage E is

A. Personal liability

B. Medical payments

C. Personal property

D. Flood

3. Homeowners Coverage F generally pays eligible medical expenses

A. Only after proving negligence

B. Without requiring proof of negligence

C. Only to the named insured

D. Only for auto accidents

Answers

1. C. Coverage D is loss of use.

2. A. Coverage E is personal liability.

3. B. Medical Payments to Others is generally no-fault coverage for eligible persons.

sections.title: Chapter 11  Personal Auto Liability and Who Is Insured
sections.html:
Chapter 11 Personal Auto Liability and Who Is Insured

Learning Objectives

Navigate PAP Parts A through F

Apply liability limits and supplementary payments

Identify covered autos and insured persons

Personal auto structure

A standard personal auto policy is organized into Part A Liability, Part B Medical Payments, Part C Uninsured Motorists, Part D Damage to Your Auto, Part E Duties After an Accident or Loss, and Part F General Provisions. Texas forms may include Personal Injury Protection and state-specific endorsements. Always identify the part before evaluating coverage.

Part A pays damages for bodily injury or property damage for which an insured becomes legally responsible because of an auto accident, subject to exclusions and limits. It also provides a defense and supplementary payments. Liability coverage protects third parties; it does not pay for injury to the named insured or physical damage to the insured own auto under Part A.

Who is an insured

For a covered auto, the named insured, resident family members, and persons using the auto with a reasonable belief they are entitled to do so may qualify. Persons or organizations legally responsible for an insured use may also qualify to the extent stated. For vehicles that are not covered autos, protection is narrower and generally follows the named insured and resident family members.

A temporary substitute replaces a covered auto that is out of normal use because of breakdown, repair, servicing, loss, or destruction. A newly acquired auto may receive automatic coverage for a limited period, but the time and breadth depend on whether it replaces an auto, is additional, and whether collision or other-than-collision coverage already exists. Prompt notice is essential.

Liability limits

Split limits such as 30 60 25 mean $30,000 bodily injury per person, $60,000 bodily injury per accident, and $25,000 property damage per accident. A combined single limit applies one amount to bodily injury and property damage together for an accident.

The per-person bodily injury limit is nested inside the per-accident limit. If three people each suffer $25,000 of bodily injury under a 30 60 policy, no person exceeds $30,000, but total payment cannot exceed $60,000. Property damage has its separate limit under split-limit coverage.

Common exclusions

Important exclusions include intentional injury, property owned or transported by an insured, property rented to used by or in the insured care subject to exceptions, use as a public or livery conveyance subject to modern sharing-network provisions, employment-related vehicle use in some circumstances, vehicles with fewer than four wheels, using a vehicle without reasonable belief of entitlement, and vehicles furnished or available for regular use but not insured under the policy.

The regular-use exclusion prevents one listed vehicle from automatically covering every vehicle routinely available to the household. A named non-owner policy or appropriate endorsement can address some exposures.

Memory Rule PAP A liability B medical payments C UM UIM D damage to your auto E duties F general provisions. Split limits are per person per accident property damage.

Chapter Review

1. Which property often needs scheduling because of theft sublimits?

A. Concrete foundation

B. Jewelry

C. Installed furnace

D. Lawn

2. A mortgagee may retain protection despite some acts of the insured because of the

A. Liberalization clause

B. Mortgage clause

C. Appraisal clause

D. Pair and set clause

3. NFIP building and contents coverage generally have

A. One combined limit only

B. Separate limits and usually separate deductibles

C. No waiting period ever

D. Automatic loss-of-use coverage

Answers

1. B. Jewelry is subject to special limits, especially for theft.

2. B. The standard mortgage clause creates separate protection subject to mortgagee duties.

3. B. NFIP building and contents are separately selected and adjusted.

sections.title: Chapter 12  Personal Auto Medical PIP UM and Physical Damage
sections.html:
Chapter 12 Personal Auto Medical PIP UM and Physical Damage

Learning Objectives

Distinguish Medical Payments from PIP

Apply UM and UIM

Separate collision from other than collision

Medical payments and PIP

Medical Payments coverage pays reasonable necessary medical and funeral expenses for covered persons after an auto accident, without requiring proof of fault, subject to time limits and exclusions. Personal Injury Protection is broader and can include medical expenses, a portion of lost income, and essential services under state law and form terms.

Texas insurers must offer PIP and UM or UIM coverage, and rejection must follow Texas requirements. The commonly tested minimum PIP offer is $2,500. Do not confuse PIP with liability. PIP benefits the insured and eligible occupants; liability protects against claims by others.

Uninsured and underinsured motorists

Uninsured motorist coverage responds when an insured is legally entitled to recover from an at-fault owner or operator who has no liability insurance or in other qualifying uninsured situations. Underinsured motorist coverage applies when the at-fault limits are insufficient for covered damages. Hit-and-run requirements depend on state law and policy wording.

UM or UIM can include bodily injury and property damage components. It does not guarantee full compensation beyond its limit and applicable offsets, deductibles, and proof requirements.

Collision and other than collision

Collision means upset of the covered auto or impact with another vehicle or object. Other than collision, historically called comprehensive, covers listed noncollision events such as fire, theft, vandalism, wind, hail, flood, contact with a bird or animal, glass breakage, falling objects, explosion, earthquake, and riot under standard wording.

The animal rule is a frequent exam item: striking a deer is other than collision. Striking a fallen tree or road debris is usually collision because the auto hits an object. Wind blowing a tree onto a parked car is other than collision.

Settlement and transportation expenses

Physical damage pays the lesser measure stated in the form, commonly actual cash value or the amount necessary to repair or replace, subject to deductible. The insurer may pay money, repair, replace, or return stolen property. Diminished value is not automatically payable merely because a repaired vehicle is worth less.

Transportation expense and rental reimbursement help with substitute transportation after a covered physical-damage loss. Waiting periods, daily limits, maximum amounts, and whether coverage applies to theft differ. Towing and labor generally requires separate coverage and pays labor performed at the place of disablement, not repair parts.

Memory Rule Collision is upset or impact. Other than collision includes theft fire hail flood glass and animal contact. Texas minimum PIP offer is commonly tested at $2,500.

Chapter Review

1. A personal articles floater is best suited for

A. Scheduled jewelry

B. Building foundations

C. Workers compensation

D. Commercial auto liability

2. A dry cleaner holding customer clothing is a

A. Mortgagor

B. Bailee

C. Surety

D. Reinsurer

3. PAP Part A provides

A. Liability

B. Medical Payments

C. Uninsured Motorists

D. Physical damage

Answers

1. A. Personal inland marine floaters schedule valuable movable property.

2. B. A bailee temporarily possesses property belonging to others.

3. A. Part A is liability coverage.

sections.title: Chapter 13  Commercial Auto and Garage Exposures
sections.html:
Chapter 13 Commercial Auto and Garage Exposures

Learning Objectives

Read business auto symbols

Distinguish owned hired and nonowned autos

Separate garagekeepers from business auto physical damage

The business auto coverage form

The Business Auto Coverage Form insures selected auto exposures using numerical covered-auto symbols. Common symbols include 1 for any auto, 2 for owned autos only, 7 for specifically described autos, 8 for hired autos, and 9 for nonowned autos. Symbol 1 is generally available for liability, not every physical-damage coverage. A question may be solved simply by matching the symbol to the vehicle.

Hired autos are vehicles leased, hired, rented, or borrowed by the named insured, subject to exceptions. Nonowned autos are vehicles the business does not own lease hire rent or borrow but that are used in its business, commonly employee-owned cars. An employee driving a personal car on a company errand creates a nonowned auto exposure for the employer.

Who is insured and liability exclusions

The named insured is an insured for any covered auto. Permissive users may be insured, but exceptions apply to owners from whom the auto is hired or borrowed, employees who own the vehicle, and parties in auto businesses. Liability exclusions include expected or intended injury, contractual liability beyond insured contracts, workers compensation, employee indemnification, care custody or control, handling property, pollution, racing, and completed operations in specified circumstances.

The individual named insured endorsement can extend certain personal-auto-type protections to an individual named insured and family members. Drive Other Car coverage addresses executives or others who need personal protection while using autos not owned by the business.

Physical damage and mobile equipment

Commercial auto physical damage may include comprehensive, specified causes of loss, and collision. Specified causes is narrower than comprehensive and lists causes such as fire, lightning, explosion, theft, windstorm, hail, earthquake, flood, vandalism, and transportation-related events.

Mobile equipment is generally land vehicles designed for off-road use or specified special functions, such as bulldozers and forklifts. CGL commonly covers mobile equipment liability, while business auto covers autos. Laws and endorsements can treat certain self-propelled equipment differently when driven on public roads.

Auto dealers and garagekeepers

Auto dealers coverage addresses liability and auto exposures of dealerships and similar businesses. Garagekeepers coverage protects customers autos left in the insured care for service, repair, parking, or storage. Legal liability coverage requires the garage to be legally liable; direct primary coverage can pay regardless of legal liability and is primary; direct excess can pay regardless of liability only above collectible customer insurance according to the form.

Do not confuse garagekeepers with CGL coverage for damage to property in the insured care, custody, or control. The specialized garagekeepers form is designed for customers vehicles.

Memory Rule Business auto symbols 1 any 2 owned 7 specifically described 8 hired 9 nonowned. Garagekeepers covers customers autos in the insured care.

Chapter Review

1. Limits 30 60 25 mean the first number is

A. Property damage per accident

B. Bodily injury per person

C. Bodily injury per accident

D. Collision deductible

2. A car used while the listed auto is being repaired is most likely a

A. Newly acquired auto

B. Temporary substitute

C. Hired commercial auto

D. Mobile equipment

3. A vehicle furnished for a family member regular use but not listed creates which concern?

A. Regular-use exclusion

B. Flood exclusion

C. Coinsurance penalty

D. Vacancy clause

Answers

1. B. The first number is bodily injury per person.

2. B. A temporary substitute replaces an out-of-use covered auto for breakdown, repair, servicing, loss, or destruction.

3. A. The regular-use exclusion prevents automatic coverage of routinely available unlisted vehicles.

sections.title: Chapter 14  Commercial Property and Causes of Loss
sections.html:
Chapter 14 Commercial Property and Causes of Loss

Learning Objectives

Identify building and business personal property

Compare Basic Broad and Special causes of loss

Apply vacancy valuation and coinsurance

The commercial property coverage part

A Commercial Package Policy combines two or more coverage parts with common declarations and conditions. Commercial property may be one part. The Building and Personal Property Coverage Form provides Building, Your Business Personal Property, and Personal Property of Others when selected and limited in the declarations.

Building includes completed additions, fixtures, permanently installed machinery and equipment, and specified property used to maintain or service the building. Business personal property generally includes furniture, machinery, stock, and other personal property owned by the insured at the described premises, plus certain tenant improvements. Property of others is a separate category in the insured care custody or control.

Causes of loss forms

The Basic Causes of Loss Form lists perils such as fire, lightning, explosion, windstorm or hail, smoke, aircraft or vehicles, riot, vandalism, sprinkler leakage, sinkhole collapse, and volcanic action, subject to wording. The Broad Form adds perils such as falling objects, weight of snow ice or sleet, and water damage from specified accidental discharge, plus additional collapse coverage. The Special Form covers direct physical loss unless excluded or limited.

Special form exclusions commonly address ordinance or law, earth movement, governmental action, nuclear hazard, utility services, war, water, fungus, electrical or mechanical breakdown, wear and tear, rust, settling, insects, faulty design or workmanship, and dishonest acts. Some excluded causes have ensuing-loss exceptions.

Additional and extension coverages

Common additional coverages include debris removal, preservation of property, fire department service charge, pollutant cleanup and removal within a sublimit, increased cost of construction within terms, and electronic data within a sublimit. Extensions may cover newly acquired property, personal effects and property of others, valuable papers and records, property off premises, outdoor property, and nonowned detached trailers when eligibility conditions are met.

Coverage extensions often require compliance with coinsurance or a stated percentage. The words additional coverage and coverage extension are not interchangeable on every question.

Vacancy and loss conditions

A commercial building is considered vacant according to different tests depending on whether the named insured is a building owner or tenant. After more than 60 consecutive days of vacancy, standard wording eliminates coverage for vandalism, sprinkler leakage unless protected, building glass breakage, water damage, theft, and attempted theft, and reduces other covered losses by 15 percent. Memorize the 60-day and 15-percent relationship.

Loss conditions address appraisal, duties, loss payment, recovered property, vacancy, and valuation. Mortgageholder provisions protect lender interests subject to lender duties. The control-of-property condition prevents acts beyond an insured direction or control from automatically defeating coverage.

Memory Rule Commercial property categories are building business personal property and personal property of others. Vacancy over 60 days removes specified losses and reduces other covered losses 15 percent.

Chapter Review

1. Striking a guardrail is generally

A. Collision

B. Other than collision

C. PIP

D. Towing only

2. Texas minimum liability limits are

A. 15 30 10

B. 25 50 25

C. 30 60 25

D. 50 100 50

3. Texas insurers must offer PIP at a commonly tested minimum of

A. $500

B. $1,000

C. $2,500

D. $10,000

Answers

1. A. Impact with an object is collision.

2. C. Texas commonly tests minimum limits of 30 60 25.

3. C. The commonly tested minimum PIP offer is $2,500.

sections.title: Chapter 15  Business Income Extra Expense Equipment Breakdown and Builders Risk
sections.html:
Chapter 15 Business Income Extra Expense Equipment Breakdown and Builders Risk

Learning Objectives

Apply business income triggers and period of restoration

Distinguish extra expense from continuing expenses

Recognize equipment breakdown and builders risk

Business income

Business income coverage replaces net income that would have been earned and continuing normal operating expenses, including payroll when covered, during a necessary suspension caused by direct physical loss from a covered cause at described premises. The coverage normally requires that the damaged property be one for which a causes-of-loss form is shown.

The period of restoration generally begins after a waiting period stated in the form and ends when property should be repaired rebuilt or replaced with reasonable speed and similar quality, or when business resumes at a new permanent location, subject to the form. It is not automatically extended because the insured delays repairs.

Extra expense and dependent property

Extra expense coverage pays necessary expenses incurred during the period of restoration that the insured would not have incurred without the loss, to avoid or minimize suspension and continue operations or reduce the business income loss. Renting temporary premises or expediting replacement equipment are typical examples.

Dependent property coverage addresses loss resulting from damage to another business on which the insured depends, such as a supplier, customer, manufacturer, or leader location that attracts customers. Civil authority, extended business income, alterations and new buildings, and utility-services endorsements address other gaps.

Equipment breakdown

Equipment breakdown coverage addresses accidental breakdown of covered equipment, including pressure, mechanical, and electrical equipment. It can cover direct property damage, expediting expenses, business income, spoilage, utility interruption, and other selected exposures. It fills gaps because ordinary wear, mechanical breakdown, electrical arcing, and pressure events may be excluded or limited under commercial property.

The event must meet the policy definition of breakdown. Maintenance problems alone are not automatically covered, and exclusions and limits still apply.

Builders risk and cyber first party

Builders risk covers buildings under construction and covered materials, supplies, fixtures, and temporary structures. Coverage commonly ends when the insured interest ends, the property is accepted, construction is completed and occupied, the building is put to intended use, or another stated termination event occurs. The form is not intended to remain permanent building insurance after completion.

Cyber first-party coverage addresses the insured own loss, such as data restoration, business interruption, cyber extortion, incident response, and notification costs. Cyber liability covers claims by third parties. Crime forms may address social engineering or funds-transfer fraud only when specifically included.

Memory Rule Business income replaces net income plus continuing expenses. Extra expense funds necessary added cost to continue or reduce suspension. Equipment breakdown covers defined accidental breakdown.

Chapter Review

1. An at-fault driver has limits too low for the insured covered damages. Which coverage is relevant?

A. Underinsured motorists

B. Collision only

C. Towing

D. Garagekeepers

2. Business auto symbol 1 means

A. Owned autos

B. Hired autos

C. Any auto

D. Specifically described autos

3. Business auto symbol 7 means

A. Any auto

B. Specifically described autos

C. Hired autos

D. Nonowned autos

Answers

1. A. UIM addresses insufficient at-fault liability limits.

2. C. Symbol 1 means any auto for eligible coverage, commonly liability.

3. B. Symbol 7 covers specifically described autos.

sections.title: Chapter 16  Commercial Package Policies and Business Owners Policies
sections.html:
Chapter 16 Commercial Package Policies and Business Owners Policies

Learning Objectives

Distinguish CPP from monoline coverage

Identify BOP eligibility and automatic features

Apply BOP property and liability sections

Commercial package structure

A Commercial Package Policy contains common declarations, common policy conditions, and two or more coverage parts. Each part has its own declarations, forms, and endorsements. Common conditions address cancellation, changes, examination of books and records, inspections and surveys, premiums, and transfer of rights and duties.

A package does not erase differences among coverage parts. Property may use one deductible and valuation method while liability uses occurrence and aggregate limits. A policy with only one coverage part is monoline, even if that part is complex.

The Business Owners Policy

A Business Owners Policy packages property and liability for eligible small to medium businesses with relatively predictable exposures. Typical eligible risks include certain offices, apartments, small mercantile operations, and service businesses within size and activity limits. Large manufacturers, high-hazard operations, and businesses requiring highly customized coverage generally do not fit.

BOP property coverage is commonly open peril subject to exclusions, and the form includes business income and extra expense more automatically than a basic commercial property arrangement. It also includes CGL-like liability, medical expenses, and supplementary payments.

BOP property concepts

The declarations identify covered buildings and business personal property. Limits, deductibles, valuation, optional coverages, and protective safeguards govern payment. Outdoor signs, money and securities, employee dishonesty, equipment breakdown, and hired or nonowned auto may require options or endorsements.

Business income under a BOP may operate on an actual-loss-sustained basis for a specified period rather than a separate dollar limit, but the exact edition controls. Exam questions identify the applicable provision.

BOP liability concepts

BOP liability covers bodily injury, property damage, and personal and advertising injury arising from covered business operations, plus medical expenses. Major exclusions resemble the CGL exclusions for expected injury, contractual obligations outside insured contracts, liquor, workers compensation, employer liability, pollution, aircraft auto or watercraft, damage to property, damage to the insured product or work, recall, and professional services.

A BOP is not the same as a personal homeowners policy and does not automatically cover every business automobile, workers compensation obligation, or professional error.

Memory Rule CPP is a framework with two or more coverage parts. BOP is a prepackaged property and liability policy for eligible lower-hazard businesses.

Chapter Review

1. Garagekeepers coverage protects

A. The garage building

B. Customers autos in the garage care

C. Employee tools only

D. Dealer advertising injury

2. In commercial property, stock owned by the insured is generally

A. Building

B. Business personal property

C. Property of others

D. Land

3. Which causes of loss form is open peril subject to exclusions?

A. Basic

B. Broad

C. Special

D. Fire only

Answers

1. B. Garagekeepers is designed for customers autos in the insured care for service, parking, or storage.

2. B. Stock is business personal property.

3. C. The Special Form covers direct physical loss unless excluded or limited.

sections.title: Chapter 17  Commercial General Liability
sections.html:
Chapter 17 Commercial General Liability

Learning Objectives

Apply CGL Coverages A B and C

Recognize occurrence and aggregate limits

Identify key exclusions and insured contracts

Coverage A

Coverage A pays sums the insured is legally obligated to pay as damages because of covered bodily injury or property damage and provides a defense against covered suits. The injury or damage must occur in the coverage territory and satisfy the occurrence or claims-made trigger. Coverage A includes premises and operations and products-completed operations exposures.

Important exclusions include expected or intended injury, most contractual liability, liquor liability for businesses in the alcohol trade, workers compensation, employer liability, pollution, aircraft auto or watercraft, mobile equipment transportation, war, damage to property in the insured care, damage to the insured product or work, impaired property, recall, and electronic data. Exceptions can restore limited coverage.

Coverage B and Coverage C

Coverage B covers personal and advertising injury caused by listed offenses. These include false arrest, detention or imprisonment; malicious prosecution; wrongful eviction or entry; oral or written publication that slanders, libels, or violates privacy; certain use of another advertising idea; and infringement of copyright, trade dress, or slogan in an advertisement, subject to exclusions.

Coverage C Medical Payments pays eligible medical expenses for accidental bodily injury on or near premises or because of operations, regardless of fault, if reported and incurred within the stated time. It excludes insureds, hired persons, tenants employees in some circumstances, workers compensation injuries, athletic participants, products-completed operations, and Coverage A exclusions as stated.

Who is an insured

Who qualifies depends on business organization. An individual named insured includes the individual and spouse for business conduct. A partnership or joint venture includes the entity and members, partners, and spouses for business conduct. An LLC includes the entity, members for business conduct, and managers for managerial duties. A corporation includes the entity, executive officers and directors for their duties, and stockholders regarding liability as stockholders. Employees and volunteer workers receive limited status for acts within duties, subject to exceptions.

Newly acquired or formed organizations may receive temporary automatic coverage if no other similar insurance exists, but not partnerships, joint ventures, or LLCs under standard provisions and not for pre-acquisition injury or damage.

Limits and supplementary payments

The each-occurrence limit applies to the total Coverage A and applicable Coverage C amounts arising from one occurrence. The general aggregate caps most covered losses other than products-completed operations, which has a separate aggregate. The personal and advertising injury limit applies per person or organization. The damage-to-premises-rented-to-you limit is a separate sublimit.

Supplementary payments can include defense expense, bail bonds, attachment bonds, reasonable insured expenses, prejudgment interest, and postjudgment interest as defined. Defense expense is commonly outside the liability limit under the standard CGL, but the form controls.

Memory Rule CGL A bodily injury and property damage. B personal and advertising injury. C medical payments. Products-completed operations has a separate aggregate.

Chapter Review

1. Which commercial property peril is added by the Broad Form over Basic?

A. Fire

B. Lightning

C. Falling objects

D. Explosion

2. Business income coverage generally includes

A. Net income plus continuing normal operating expenses

B. Only property repair

C. Only extra advertising

D. Only employee theft

3. Renting temporary premises to continue operations is most directly

A. Extra expense

B. Coinsurance

C. Subrogation

D. Salvage

Answers

1. C. Falling objects is a Broad Form addition.

2. A. Business income combines net income that would have been earned and continuing operating expense.

3. A. It is an added expense incurred to continue operations and reduce suspension.

sections.title: Chapter 18  Workers Compensation and Employers Liability
sections.html:
Chapter 18 Workers Compensation and Employers Liability

Learning Objectives

Distinguish Part One from Part Two

Explain exclusive remedy and workers compensation benefits

Understand premium classification and other states coverage

The policy

Part One Workers Compensation Insurance pays benefits required by the workers compensation law of states listed in the information page. Benefits are statutory, so Part One does not show an ordinary dollar limit. Part Two Employers Liability covers specified employee injury claims outside the workers compensation benefit system and uses bodily injury by accident and bodily injury by disease limits.

Part Three Other States Insurance can provide temporary protection when operations begin in a state listed in the policy for which coverage was not known at inception, subject to notice and form conditions. It does not replace known exposure that should have been scheduled.

Benefits and exclusive remedy

Workers compensation provides medical, income, rehabilitation, death, and burial benefits according to state law. Benefits generally apply without requiring the employee to prove employer negligence. In exchange, workers compensation is usually the employee exclusive remedy against a subscribing employer for covered injury, subject to statutory exceptions.

Employers liability may cover third-party-over actions, loss of consortium, dual-capacity claims, and consequential bodily injury to relatives when the policy conditions are met. It does not duplicate benefits payable under Part One.

Premium and experience

Premium begins with payroll or another exposure base multiplied by the rate for each classification, usually per $100 of payroll. It is adjusted by experience modification, schedule credits or debits when allowed, expense constants, and other factors. Because payroll and classifications can change, the initial premium is a deposit subject to audit.

An experience modification above 1.00 generally increases premium; below 1.00 generally decreases it. It compares actual loss experience with expected loss experience for similar operations, adjusted under rating rules.

Federal and special exposures

Ordinary state workers compensation may not cover every worker. Federal programs include the Federal Employers Liability Act for qualifying railroad workers and the U.S. Longshore and Harbor Workers Compensation Act for qualifying maritime employment. The Jones Act affects seamen. Endorsements or specialized policies address these exposures.

Independent contractor status depends on law and actual relationship, not merely a label. Questions may focus on who controls the work and whether the person fits the legal definition of employee.

Memory Rule Part One pays statutory workers compensation. Part Two is employers liability. Part Three is other states. Premium is auditable and classification based.

Chapter Review

1. Builders risk coverage is designed for

A. Completed occupied buildings indefinitely

B. Buildings under construction

C. Employee injury

D. Customer autos

2. A CPP must generally contain

A. Only one coverage part

B. Two or more coverage parts

C. Only homeowners coverage

D. Only workers compensation

3. A BOP is primarily intended for

A. Eligible smaller lower-hazard businesses

B. Every multinational manufacturer

C. Personal automobiles

D. Ocean vessels

Answers

1. B. Builders risk covers construction-phase property.

2. B. A package combines two or more coverage parts with common elements.

3. A. BOP eligibility focuses on relatively predictable small-business exposures.

sections.title: Chapter 19  Crime Insurance Fidelity and Surety Bonds
sections.html:
Chapter 19 Crime Insurance Fidelity and Surety Bonds

Learning Objectives

Distinguish theft burglary robbery and mysterious disappearance

Separate discovery and loss sustained forms

Compare fidelity with surety bonds

Crime definitions

Theft is the broad taking of property. Burglary generally requires unlawful taking from inside premises with visible signs of forcible entry or exit under older defined-peril concepts. Robbery involves taking property from a person by force or threat. Mysterious disappearance is unexplained loss with no proof of what happened and is not automatically theft.

Forgery or alteration coverage addresses specified instruments. Computer fraud, funds transfer fraud, social engineering, money orders and counterfeit currency, and employee theft are separate insuring agreements. One does not automatically substitute for another.

Employee theft

Employee theft coverage protects the employer against covered theft committed by an employee, often whether acting alone or in collusion. The definition of employee and termination-as-to-employee condition are important. Knowledge of a prior dishonest act can end or prevent coverage for that employee.

A discovery form covers loss discovered during the policy period or extended discovery period, even if the act occurred earlier subject to prior-loss provisions. A loss-sustained form generally requires the loss to occur during the policy period and be discovered within a stated period after expiration.

Fidelity bonds

A fidelity bond is a two-party arrangement in practical effect that protects an employer from employee dishonesty. It resembles crime insurance. Blanket positions or employee arrangements may cover groups, while name-schedule arrangements identify individuals.

A public official bond and financial institution bond address specialized fidelity risks. The examination distinction is purpose: fidelity protects the employer or obligee from dishonest conduct.

Surety bonds

Suretyship involves three parties. The principal promises performance, the obligee requires and receives the guarantee, and the surety guarantees the principal obligation. If the surety pays because the principal defaults, the surety generally seeks reimbursement from the principal. Unlike insurance, suretyship expects no loss.

Contract bonds include bid, performance, and payment bonds. License and permit bonds guarantee compliance with law. Court bonds support judicial duties or obligations. A bid bond supports entry into a contract; a performance bond supports completion; a payment bond supports payment of subcontractors and suppliers.

Memory Rule Surety has principal obligee and surety. Fidelity protects against dishonesty. Robbery uses force or threat; burglary uses defined forcible entry; mysterious disappearance is unexplained.

Chapter Review

1. CGL Coverage B applies to

A. Workers compensation

B. Personal and advertising injury

C. Building damage only

D. Auto physical damage

2. CGL Coverage C is

A. Medical Payments

B. Business income

C. Crime

D. Professional liability

3. A claim arising after work is finished is most likely which exposure?

A. Premises only

B. Products-completed operations

C. Medical payments only

D. Inland marine

Answers

1. B. Coverage B covers listed personal and advertising injury offenses.

2. A. Coverage C provides medical payments for eligible accidental injuries.

3. B. Completed work falls within products-completed operations.

sections.title: Chapter 20  Professional Umbrella and Specialty Liability
sections.html:
Chapter 20 Professional Umbrella and Specialty Liability

Learning Objectives

Identify professional liability forms

Separate umbrella from excess liability

Recognize cyber liquor D and O and EPLI exposures

Professional liability

Professional liability covers errors, omissions, or wrongful acts arising from professional services. Examples include medical malpractice, agents errors and omissions, accountants liability, architects and engineers liability, and lawyers professional liability. These policies are often claims made and may use defense-within-limits wording, consent-to-settle clauses, retroactive dates, and extended reporting periods.

A consent-to-settle provision may require the insured approval before settlement. A hammer clause can limit the insurer responsibility if the insured refuses a recommended settlement and the final outcome is worse.

Directors officers and employment practices

Directors and Officers liability covers wrongful acts in managing an organization and may protect individual directors and officers, reimburse the organization for indemnification, and cover the entity for specified claims. It does not insure every poor business result or deliberate illegal gain.

Employment Practices Liability Insurance addresses claims such as discrimination, harassment, wrongful termination, and retaliation. Workers compensation covers occupational injury, not employment-practices allegations. Employee benefits liability addresses certain errors in administering benefit programs.

Cyber and liquor liability

Cyber liability covers third-party claims involving privacy, network security, and media liability. Cyber first party covers the insured response cost, data restoration, interruption, extortion, and related loss when scheduled. Precise definitions, waiting periods, sublimits, vendor events, and social-engineering endorsements matter.

Liquor liability covers liability arising from causing or contributing to intoxication, furnishing alcohol to minors, or violating alcohol laws. A CGL host-liquor exception may protect a business that is not in the business of manufacturing, selling, serving, or furnishing alcohol. Bars and restaurants need liquor liability coverage.

Umbrella and excess
