Excess liability adds limits above scheduled underlying insurance and usually follows the underlying coverage more closely. A commercial umbrella can provide higher limits and may cover some claims not covered by underlying policies, subject to a self-insured retention and its own exclusions. Drop-down coverage is not automatic for every gap.

The umbrella requires maintenance of underlying limits. Failure to maintain them generally leaves the insured responsible for the gap rather than making the umbrella pay from the first dollar.

Memory Rule Professional liability often uses claims made. EPLI covers employment claims. Umbrella may be broader; excess usually follows underlying coverage. Underlying limits must be maintained.

Chapter Review

1. A bar liability for serving an intoxicated patron is primarily addressed by

A. Host liquor only

B. Liquor liability

C. Homeowners

D. Inland marine

2. Workers compensation Part One pays

A. Statutory benefits

B. Professional liability

C. Auto collision

D. Punitive damages only

3. Workers compensation Part Two is

A. Employers Liability

B. Other States

C. Property

D. Crime

Answers

1. B. Businesses in the alcohol trade need liquor liability; the CGL liquor exclusion applies.

2. A. Part One pays benefits required by listed state workers compensation law.

3. A. Part Two provides employers liability coverage.

sections.title: Chapter 21  Texas Insurance Regulation and Insurer Types
sections.html:
Chapter 21 Texas Insurance Regulation and Insurer Types

Learning Objectives

Understand TDI and Commissioner authority

Classify domestic foreign alien stock and mutual insurers

Separate admitted and nonadmitted markets

Texas Department of Insurance

The Texas Department of Insurance administers and enforces the Insurance Code and rules. The Commissioner of Insurance has authority to examine insurers, investigate conduct, hold hearings, issue orders, impose or seek authorized penalties, and protect the public within statutory authority. Examination questions ask which official has a power, not whether an agent personally agrees with an enforcement decision.

A certificate of authority permits an insurer to transact authorized insurance in Texas. Transacting insurance includes activities such as soliciting, negotiating, effecting contracts, and other acts defined by law. Producers need licenses; insurers need authority unless a lawful nonadmitted placement applies.

Insurer classifications

A domestic insurer is formed under Texas law. A foreign insurer is formed under another U.S. state or jurisdiction. An alien insurer is formed under the law of another country. These terms describe domicile, not ownership or quality.

A stock insurer is owned by stockholders. A mutual insurer is owned by policyholders. A reciprocal exchange consists of subscribers who exchange insurance through an attorney-in-fact. Texas Lloyds is an authorized form of insurer operating under Texas law and should not be confused automatically with Lloyds of London.

Admitted and nonadmitted

An admitted or authorized insurer holds a Texas certificate of authority. A nonadmitted insurer does not. Eligible surplus lines insurance may be placed with an eligible nonadmitted insurer through properly licensed surplus lines channels when the risk cannot be obtained from admitted markets under applicable requirements.

Guaranty association protection generally relates to covered claims of member admitted insurers and ordinarily does not protect surplus lines policies. Producers must not imply that a nonadmitted insurer is unauthorized in the sense of an illegal placement when the surplus lines transaction is lawful.

Rating and forms

Texas law governs how insurers file and use rates, rules, and policy forms. Some systems allow use after filing unless disapproved; others require prior approval or have special rules. The exam outline expects candidates to know that TDI regulates unfairly discriminatory, excessive, inadequate, or unlawful practices within statutory standards.

A producer does not have authority to invent rates, waive filed requirements, or alter forms without insurer authorization. Quoting and binding must follow the appointment, underwriting guidelines, and filed or approved materials.

Memory Rule Domestic means Texas. Foreign means another state. Alien means another country. Admitted insurers hold a certificate of authority.

Chapter Review

1. Workers compensation premium is commonly based on rate per

A. $100 of payroll

B. $1 of property value

C. $1,000 of sales only

D. Vehicle

2. Taking property from a person by force is

A. Burglary

B. Robbery

C. Mysterious disappearance

D. Forgery

3. Unexplained missing property without evidence of theft is

A. Robbery

B. Burglary

C. Mysterious disappearance

D. Subrogation

Answers

1. A. Classification rates commonly apply per $100 of payroll.

2. B. Robbery involves force or threat against a person.

3. C. Mysterious disappearance is unexplained and not automatically theft.

sections.title: Chapter 22  Texas Producer Licensing Appointments and Records
sections.html:
Chapter 22 Texas Producer Licensing Appointments and Records

Learning Objectives

Apply individual agency and temporary licensing rules

Understand appointment and commission restrictions

Remember renewal CE and reporting duties

Individual licensing

A Texas resident applicant for the General Lines Property and Casualty license must generally be at least 18, pass the required examination, complete fingerprint requirements, submit the application and fee, and meet suitability requirements. The application must be submitted within one year after passing or the examination must be retaken. The current TDI application fee is $50.

A one-time 180-day temporary general lines license may be available through a sponsoring insurer, agent, or agency. The sponsor must request it, supervise training, and provide at least 40 hours of training within the required period. The candidate must pass the examination within the temporary term to obtain permanent authority through that path.

Agency licensing

An entity acting as an insurance agency needs the appropriate agency license. A Texas resident P&C agency identifies a designated responsible licensed producer who is an officer or active partner holding the Texas General Lines P&C license. People who personally perform producer acts also need individual authority.

TDI currently requires resident agency proof of financial responsibility through a $25,000 bond or a $250,000 errors and omissions policy with a deductible no greater than 10 percent of the policy amount. The legal entity name must match the bond or policy.

Appointments and commissions

A license establishes legal qualification; an appointment establishes the relationship through which a producer represents an insurer. Producers must act within license and appointment authority. An insurer is responsible for appointment filings and termination notices under applicable rules.

Commission may generally be paid only as permitted by licensing law. A person cannot evade licensing by calling sales compensation a referral fee. Purely clerical referrals without discussion of terms may be treated differently under specific law, but examination questions usually reject payment of insurance commission to an unlicensed person for selling, soliciting, or negotiating.

Renewal education and records

Texas individual licenses are generally renewed every two years. The General Lines P&C license requires 24 hours of continuing education per license period, including 3 hours of ethics, with at least half completed through classroom or classroom-equivalent instruction unless an exemption applies. Deficiency can produce fines and prevent renewal.

A license holder must keep required records, protect premiums and client information, update TDI as required, and report specified criminal or administrative matters. Use the period stated in the question; the exam outline cites Texas Insurance Code Sections 4001.252 and 4001.255 and related rules. When studying changing deadlines, verify the current TDI text shortly before the exam.

Memory Rule Age 18. Apply within one year after passing. Temporary license 180 days with 40 hours sponsor training. CE is 24 hours including 3 ethics every two years.

Chapter Review

1. The party requiring a surety guarantee is the

A. Obligee

B. Principal

C. Adjuster

D. Reinsurer

2. Which bond guarantees contract completion?

A. Bid bond

B. Performance bond

C. Payment bond

D. Fidelity bond

3. A claims-made professional liability policy may use a

A. Retroactive date

B. Coinsurance percentage only

C. Flood waiting period

D. Auto symbol

Answers

1. A. The obligee receives the guarantee.

2. B. A performance bond guarantees performance of the contract.

3. A. The retroactive date limits how far back covered wrongful acts may occur.

sections.title: Chapter 23  Texas Unfair Practices and Producer Conduct
sections.html:
Chapter 23 Texas Unfair Practices and Producer Conduct

Learning Objectives

Recognize misrepresentation rebating and defamation

Separate coercion discrimination and controlled business

Apply fiduciary standards to premiums and claims

Misrepresentation and advertising

Misrepresentation includes false or misleading statements about policy terms, benefits, dividends, financial condition, or competitors, and misleading comparisons intended to induce a transaction. False advertising uses untrue, deceptive, or misleading statements in advertising. A producer must accurately identify the insurer, policy, limitations, and personal role.

Defamation is a false maliciously critical or derogatory statement calculated to injure an insurer or person in the insurance business. Truthful comparison based on reliable facts is different from defamation.

Rebating and inducements

Rebating involves offering an unlawful valuable consideration or inducement not specified in the policy to persuade a person to buy insurance. Returning part of commission, giving an unfiled benefit, or offering a special favor unavailable on the same terms can be a rebate. Lawful advertising items or programs must fit statutory and regulatory conditions.

Twisting is misrepresentation or incomplete comparison used to induce replacement. Churning uses existing policy values to generate a new transaction for producer benefit without appropriate client benefit. Although these terms are common in life insurance, the underlying prohibition on deception applies broadly.

Coercion discrimination and controlled business

Boycott, coercion, and intimidation use pressure or concerted action to restrain insurance trade or force a transaction. A lender may require adequate insurance but generally cannot unlawfully force purchase from one particular agent when acceptable coverage is available elsewhere.

Unfair discrimination treats similar risks differently without a lawful actuarial or underwriting basis or uses prohibited characteristics. Controlled business refers to insurance written primarily on the producer own interests, relatives, employer, or associated interests and can show that a license is sought without genuine public insurance activity.

Claims and fiduciary conduct

Unfair claims practices include knowingly misrepresenting relevant facts or policy provisions, failing to acknowledge or act reasonably promptly, failing to conduct a reasonable investigation, refusing a claim without reasonable investigation, and failing to attempt a prompt fair settlement when liability is reasonably clear, subject to statutory wording.

Premium funds received in a fiduciary capacity must be handled according to law and agreement. Conversion, commingling where prohibited, false entries, backdating, forged signatures, and unauthorized policy changes can lead to discipline and criminal exposure.

Memory Rule Misrepresentation concerns policy or transaction facts. Defamation injures reputation. Rebating offers an unlisted inducement. Coercion forces a transaction.

Chapter Review

1. An umbrella self-insured retention may apply when

A. The underlying policy covers the loss

B. The umbrella covers a claim not covered by underlying insurance

C. The property is vacant

D. Workers compensation benefits are due

2. A domestic insurer in Texas is formed under the laws of

A. Any U.S. state

B. Texas

C. Another country

D. The federal government only

3. An insurer formed in Oklahoma is what type in Texas?

A. Domestic

B. Foreign

C. Alien

D. Reciprocal only

Answers

1. B. An SIR commonly applies to an umbrella-covered claim without underlying coverage.

2. B. Domestic refers to the insurer state of formation.

3. B. Another U.S. state makes it foreign in Texas.

sections.title: Chapter 24  Texas Homeowners FAIR Plan and Windstorm Rules
sections.html:
Chapter 24 Texas Homeowners FAIR Plan and Windstorm Rules

Learning Objectives

Identify residual market purposes

Understand cancellation and nonrenewal concepts

Recognize TWIA and prompt property claim rules

Homeowners cancellation and nonrenewal

Cancellation ends a policy before its expiration; nonrenewal means the insurer declines a new term at expiration. Texas restricts permissible cancellation after an initial underwriting period and requires advance written notice. Nonpayment, fraud or material misrepresentation, increased hazard within the insured control, and specified legal grounds are common cancellation bases. Nonrenewal follows separate notice and underwriting rules.

Notice periods and protected circumstances can change by statute. Learn the distinction and verify the current numerical deadlines in the official Texas materials immediately before the examination. A notice must comply with delivery, timing, and reason requirements applicable to the policy.

Texas FAIR Plan Association

The Texas FAIR Plan Association provides limited basic residential property insurance to eligible applicants who cannot obtain coverage in the voluntary market. It is a residual market, not a competitor intended to replace available private insurance. Applicants generally must show unsuccessful efforts in the voluntary market and meet property and underwriting requirements.

FAIR Plan coverage may be narrower and costlier than standard homeowners coverage. It does not guarantee acceptance of an uninsurable property or every optional coverage.

Texas Windstorm Insurance Association

TWIA provides wind and hail coverage for eligible property in designated coastal catastrophe areas when coverage is unavailable in the voluntary market. The underlying homeowners or commercial property policy may exclude wind and hail. TWIA is therefore commonly paired with another policy that covers fire and other perils.

Eligibility may depend on location, construction standards, inspections, certificates of compliance, and declinations from voluntary insurers. Flood remains separate from TWIA wind and hail coverage.

Property claims and settlement

Texas prompt-payment law imposes timelines for acknowledging claims, requesting reasonably necessary information, accepting or rejecting claims, and paying accepted claims, with extensions and catastrophe rules. The exact application depends on claim type and circumstances. Producers should promptly transmit notices and never promise that a claim will be paid.

Replacement cost provisions generally require actual repair or replacement before full recoverable depreciation is paid. A liquidated-demand rule may apply to specified total fire losses on real property, but it does not convert every property loss into automatic policy-limit payment.

Memory Rule FAIR Plan is residual residential property. TWIA is eligible coastal wind and hail. Flood is separate. Cancellation and nonrenewal are different legal actions.

Chapter Review

1. An admitted insurer has a Texas

A. Certificate of authority

B. Surplus lines stamp only

C. Real estate license

D. Workers compensation claim

2. Which organization is owned by policyholders?

A. Stock insurer

B. Mutual insurer

C. Agency LLC

D. Adjusting firm

3. A Texas resident individual must generally apply within what time after passing the P&C exam?

A. 30 days

B. 90 days

C. One year

D. Two years

Answers

1. A. The certificate authorizes the insurer to transact admitted insurance.

2. B. Mutual insurers are owned by their policyholders.

3. C. The current licensing guidance gives one year.

sections.title: Chapter 25  Texas Automobile Insurance Rules
sections.html:
Chapter 25 Texas Automobile Insurance Rules

Learning Objectives

Memorize Texas minimum liability limits

Apply PIP and UM UIM offer rules

Recognize TAIPA and rideshare gaps

Financial responsibility

Texas drivers must demonstrate financial responsibility. The minimum auto liability limits commonly tested are 30 60 25: $30,000 bodily injury per person, $60,000 bodily injury per accident, and $25,000 property damage per accident. These minimums can be inadequate for a serious crash, but the examination asks what law requires, not what an adviser recommends.

An insurance card or authorized electronic proof can demonstrate coverage. Failure to maintain financial responsibility can result in legal penalties and vehicle-related consequences.

PIP and UM UIM

Texas auto insurers must offer Personal Injury Protection, commonly tested with a minimum offer of $2,500, unless rejected in writing by the named insured. PIP can pay covered medical expenses, a percentage of lost income, and essential services without regard to fault under the form.

Uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage must also be offered and requires a written rejection. It protects insureds who are legally entitled to recover from an uninsured or underinsured motorist, subject to limits and terms. A producer should retain valid rejection documentation.

Cancellation nonrenewal and assigned risk

Texas regulates cancellation and nonrenewal of personal auto insurance, including notice and permissible reasons. A new policy may permit broader underwriting cancellation during its initial period than a renewal policy. Nonpayment generally permits shorter notice. Use the facts and current rule stated in exam preparation materials because deadlines can change.

The Texas Automobile Insurance Plan Association provides access to required auto liability coverage for eligible applicants unable to obtain insurance in the voluntary market. TAIPA is an assigned-risk mechanism and does not exist to provide the broadest or least expensive policy.

Transportation network companies

Personal auto policies commonly exclude or restrict coverage while a vehicle is available for hire or used to carry passengers for compensation. Texas law and transportation network company coverage divide the exposure among periods such as app off, app on awaiting a request, and passenger trip. Company-provided coverage and personal endorsements must be coordinated.

The same issue appears with delivery platforms. A personal policy does not automatically become business auto coverage merely because the driver uses a personal vehicle.

Memory Rule Texas minimum auto liability is 30 60 25. PIP minimum offer is $2,500. PIP and UM UIM may be rejected only through the required written process.

Chapter Review

1. A temporary general lines license is issued for a one-time term of

A. 30 days

B. 90 days

C. 180 days

D. Two years

2. Sponsor training for a temporary Texas general lines license is at least

A. 8 hours

B. 24 hours

C. 40 hours

D. 60 hours

3. Texas General Lines P&C continuing education is generally

A. 10 hours yearly

B. 24 hours per two-year period including 3 ethics

C. 40 hours every four years

D. No CE

Answers

1. C. The temporary license is a one-time 180-day license.

2. C. Texas requires at least 40 hours of sponsor-provided training.

3. B. The standard requirement is 24 hours per license period with 3 ethics hours.

sections.title: Chapter 26  Texas Workers Compensation Surplus Lines and Guaranty Systems
sections.html:
Chapter 26 Texas Workers Compensation Surplus Lines and Guaranty Systems

Learning Objectives

Understand Texas subscriber and nonsubscriber concepts

Identify lawful surplus lines placement

Distinguish guaranty and medical liability market mechanisms

Texas workers compensation

Most private Texas employers may choose whether to subscribe to workers compensation, subject to important exceptions and notice requirements. A subscriber purchases authorized workers compensation coverage and receives statutory protections, including exclusive-remedy protection for most covered claims. A nonsubscriber may face employee negligence suits and loses important common-law defenses under Texas law.

Covered benefits include medical, temporary income, impairment income, supplemental income, lifetime income for specified catastrophic injuries, death, and burial benefits as applicable. The Texas Department of Insurance Division of Workers Compensation administers the system.

Surplus lines

Surplus lines insurance provides access to coverage for risks that admitted insurers will not write. It is placed through a licensed surplus lines agent with an eligible nonadmitted insurer after required diligent search or other eligibility rules are satisfied. The policy must include required disclosures, taxes, and stamping or reporting procedures.

A General Lines P&C license alone does not grant authority to act as a surplus lines agent. Separate surplus lines licensing is required. Nonadmitted policies generally do not receive Texas guaranty association protection.

Property and casualty guaranty association

The Texas Property and Casualty Insurance Guaranty Association handles eligible covered claims when a member insurer becomes impaired or insolvent, subject to statutory limits, exclusions, residency, timing, and claim requirements. It is a safety net, not an insurer that agents may use as a sales inducement.

Surplus lines insurers, self-insurance arrangements, and certain specialized coverages may fall outside guaranty protection. Never promise protection without checking the statute.

Medical liability underwriting association

The Texas Medical Liability Insurance Underwriting Association, often called the JUA, provides a market mechanism for eligible health care providers unable to obtain medical liability insurance in the voluntary market. It is distinct from the guaranty association and from workers compensation.

Residual mechanisms solve availability problems: FAIR Plan for eligible residential property, TWIA for eligible coastal wind and hail, TAIPA for assigned-risk auto, and the medical liability JUA for eligible medical professional liability.

Memory Rule Texas private employers may often choose subscriber status. Surplus lines uses eligible nonadmitted insurers and a separate license. Residual plans address availability.

Chapter Review

1. A false statement intended to injure an insurer reputation is

A. Defamation

B. Coinsurance

C. Controlled business

D. Retention

2. Paying sales commission to an unlicensed person for negotiating coverage is generally

A. Required

B. Prohibited

C. A form of reinsurance

D. A claims practice

3. Which Texas market addresses eligible applicants unable to obtain residential property coverage voluntarily?

A. FAIR Plan

B. TAIPA

C. JUA

D. NFIP only

Answers

1. A. Defamation harms reputation through false derogatory statements.

2. B. Selling, soliciting, and negotiating require licensing, and commission sharing is restricted.

3. A. The Texas FAIR Plan is a residential property residual market.

sections.title: Chapter 27  Insurance Math and Exam Calculations
sections.html:
Chapter 27 Insurance Math and Exam Calculations

Learning Objectives

Calculate ACV coinsurance and liability limits

Compute premium and pro rata cancellation

Avoid common arithmetic traps

Actual cash value

Use ACV equals replacement cost minus depreciation unless the question supplies a different definition. If a five-year-old roof component costs $20,000 to replace and has accumulated 40 percent depreciation, depreciation is $8,000 and ACV is $12,000. Apply the deductible after determining the covered amount unless the question directs otherwise.

Do not depreciate land. Do not pay more than the applicable limit or covered interest.

Coinsurance

First calculate required insurance: value times coinsurance percentage. Then divide insurance carried by insurance required. Multiply that ratio by the covered loss and subtract the deductible. If carried insurance meets or exceeds the requirement, no coinsurance penalty applies, but the deductible and limit still do.

Example: value $800,000, requirement 80 percent, carried $480,000, loss $200,000, deductible $2,000. Required is $640,000. Ratio is 0.75. The amount before deductible is $150,000; after deductible it is $148,000.

Liability limits

For 50 100 25 split limits, each injured person is capped at $50,000, everyone combined is capped at $100,000, and property damage is capped at $25,000. Apply the per-person caps first, then the accident cap. A $300,000 combined single limit uses one total for covered bodily injury and property damage arising from the accident.

Aggregate limits reduce as covered amounts are paid during the policy period. A $1 million occurrence limit does not override a $2 million aggregate after that aggregate is exhausted.

Premium calculations and cancellation

A rate of $2.40 per $100 of payroll applied to $500,000 payroll produces $12,000 manual premium: $500,000 divided by $100, multiplied by $2.40. An experience modification of 0.90 produces $10,800 before other charges.

Pro rata cancellation returns the exact unearned portion without penalty. Short-rate cancellation returns less than pro rata and therefore includes a penalty, commonly when the insured cancels. Flat cancellation treats the policy as if it never took effect and returns all premium when permitted. The policy and law determine which method applies.

Memory Rule ACV equals replacement cost minus depreciation. Coinsurance is carried divided by required times loss minus deductible. Apply per-person limits before per-accident limits.

Chapter Review

1. Most private Texas employers may generally

A. Never buy workers compensation

B. Choose whether to subscribe, subject to exceptions and notice rules

C. Avoid all employee liability

D. Use homeowners instead

2. A Texas nonsubscriber generally loses important

A. Common-law defenses

B. Property deductibles

C. Auto symbols

D. Flood limits

3. Surplus lines coverage is placed with

A. Only admitted insurers

B. Eligible nonadmitted insurers through licensed channels

C. The FAIR Plan only

D. Any unlicensed person

Answers

1. B. Texas permits many private employers to choose subscriber status, unlike most states.

2. A. Nonsubscribers face negligence suits without important traditional defenses.

3. B. Surplus lines is a regulated placement with eligible nonadmitted insurers.

sections.title: Chapter 28  Final Review and Test Day Strategy
sections.html:
Chapter 28 Final Review and Test Day Strategy

Learning Objectives

Prioritize high-yield distinctions

Use time efficiently

Convert mistakes into last-minute review

High yield comparisons

Know HO 3 versus HO 5, DP 2 versus DP 3, collision versus other than collision, PIP versus medical payments, UM versus UIM, occurrence versus claims made, CGL Coverage A versus B, BOP versus CPP, fidelity versus surety, and FAIR Plan versus TWIA. These pairs produce many scenario questions.

For state law, know 30 60 25 auto limits, the $2,500 PIP offer, written rejection concepts, the 24-hour CE requirement including 3 ethics hours, the one-year post-exam application period, the 180-day temporary license, and the purpose of each residual market.

The two pass method

On the first pass, answer questions you can solve confidently and flag those requiring calculation or close comparison. Do not spend four minutes protecting one question while leaving easier questions unseen. On the second pass, eliminate clearly wrong options, apply the relevant form, and make the best supported choice. Answer every item because unanswered questions cannot earn credit and there is no benefit to trying to identify pretest questions.

With 150 minutes and approximately 145 presented questions under the current outline, average time is slightly more than one minute per question. Preserve at least 15 minutes to revisit flagged items.

How to review a missed question

Classify each miss as a knowledge gap, form confusion, reading mistake, or math mistake. A knowledge gap requires rereading. Form confusion requires a comparison chart. A reading mistake requires slowing down around words such as except, least, first, and most. A math mistake requires writing the formula before inserting numbers.

Do not memorize only an answer letter. State the governing rule aloud, create a new example, and explain why each distractor fails.

Exam day

Use the exact legal name shown on acceptable government identification when registering. Arrive early and follow the current Pearson VUE identification and testing rules. The current handbook permits only specified silent handheld nonprinting calculators without an alphabetic keypad and prohibits financial calculators. Verify the current rules before test day.

Sleep and ordinary meals matter more than last-minute cramming. Review memory pages and Texas numbers, then stop. The goal is accurate recognition and application, not recall of every sentence in this book.

Memory Rule Read the last sentence first. Identify form coverage trigger exclusion exception limit deductible and condition. Answer every question and reserve time for review.

Chapter Review

1. A rate of $3 per $100 applied to $200,000 payroll equals

A. $600

B. $3,000

C. $6,000

D. $60,000

2. Pro rata cancellation means

A. The insurer keeps all premium

B. Unearned premium is returned without a cancellation penalty

C. The insured receives less than the exact unearned amount

D. Coverage never began in every case

3. Short-rate cancellation generally

A. Includes a penalty

B. Returns all premium

C. Increases policy limits

D. Waives the deductible

Answers

1. C. $200,000 divided by $100 is 2,000 units; 2,000 times $3 is $6,000.

2. B. Pro rata returns the proportional unearned premium.

3. A. Short rate returns less than pro rata, commonly when the insured cancels.

sections.title: Practice Examination
sections.html:
Practice Examination

Allow 150 minutes for this 145-question full-length practice examination. It mirrors the current total number of scoreable and pretest questions, although every question here should be answered and reviewed. Choose the best answer. Do not view the explanations until you finish.

Answer Key and Explanations

1. B Pure risk has the possibility of loss or no loss and is generally the type insurance addresses.

2. C Faulty wiring is a tangible condition that increases the chance of fire.

3. B Dishonest intent is a moral hazard.

4. B Sprinklers reduce the severity of a possible fire.

5. C More similar exposure units improve the reliability of aggregate loss predictions.

6. B The applicant consideration includes premium and application representations.

7. C An uncertain event determines whether and how much the insurer pays.

8. B Declarations personalize the policy with names, limits, dates, and covered locations or property.

9. B An endorsement modifies the contract and controls over conflicting standard wording.

10. B A binder provides temporary insurance subject to its terms.

11. B ACV is commonly calculated as replacement cost minus depreciation: $30,000 minus $9,000.

12. B Blanket insurance applies one limit across more than one item, type, or location.

13. B $400,000 multiplied by 80 percent equals $320,000.

14. C The exam formula applies the coinsurance ratio to the loss and then subtracts the deductible.

15. B Proximate cause is the dominant cause producing the loss sequence.

16. D Negligence requires duty, breach, causation, and damages.

17. B Vicarious liability arises from a legally recognized relationship.

18. B Special damages are measurable economic losses.

19. A General damages are noneconomic losses.

20. B The retroactive date bars coverage for wrongful acts before the stated date.

21. B Appraisal determines amount, not the coverage question.

22. B Subrogation transfers recovery rights to the paying insurer to the extent of payment.

23. A The Fair Credit Reporting Act governs consumer reports and adverse-action notice.

24. C The insured must take reasonable steps to protect damaged property.

25. B Potentially covered allegations may trigger defense even when indemnity is ultimately not owed.

26. A DP 1 is the Basic Form.

27. B DP 3 gives open-peril protection to the dwelling and structures, while contents remain named peril.

28. B It replaces covered rental value lost during uninhabitability, net of noncontinuing expenses.

29. C Liability is added rather than automatically packaged in the basic dwelling form.

30. B Unoccupied normally means contents remain but people are absent.

31. B HO 4 is the tenants or contents broad form.

32. C HO 6 is the unit-owners form.

33. B HO 3 is open peril for the dwelling and other structures and named peril for contents.

34. B HO 5 generally broadens personal property to open peril.

35. B HO 8 addresses certain older homes where replacement cost may be disproportionate.

36. A Coverage A is the dwelling.

37. C Coverage D is loss of use.

38. A Coverage E is personal liability.

39. B Medical Payments to Others is generally no-fault coverage for eligible persons.

40. C Standard homeowners policies exclude flood.

41. B Jewelry is subject to special limits, especially for theft.

42. B The standard mortgage clause creates separate protection subject to mortgagee duties.

43. B NFIP building and contents are separately selected and adjusted.

44. B TWIA provides eligible coastal wind and hail coverage.

45. A Personal inland marine floaters schedule valuable movable property.

46. B A bailee temporarily possesses property belonging to others.

47. A Part A is liability coverage.

48. C Part D covers physical damage to covered autos.

49. B The first number is bodily injury per person.

50. B A temporary substitute replaces an out-of-use covered auto for breakdown, repair, servicing, loss, or destruction.

51. A The regular-use exclusion prevents automatic coverage of routinely available unlisted vehicles.

52. B Animal contact is treated as other than collision.

53. A Impact with an object is collision.

54. C Texas commonly tests minimum limits of 30 60 25.

55. C The commonly tested minimum PIP offer is $2,500.

56. B PIP provides first-party benefits under its terms.

57. A UIM addresses insufficient at-fault liability limits.

58. C Symbol 1 means any auto for eligible coverage, commonly liability.

59. B Symbol 7 covers specifically described autos.

60. B The business does not own or hire it, so it is a nonowned auto exposure.

61. B Garagekeepers is designed for customers autos in the insured care for service, parking, or storage.

62. B Stock is business personal property.

63. C The Special Form covers direct physical loss unless excluded or limited.

64. C Standard commercial wording applies a 15 percent reduction to other covered losses after the vacancy threshold.

65. C Falling objects is a Broad Form addition.

66. A Business income combines net income that would have been earned and continuing operating expense.

67. A It is an added expense incurred to continue operations and reduce suspension.

68. A The coverage fills mechanical, electrical, and pressure-equipment gaps.

69. B Builders risk covers construction-phase property.

70. B A package combines two or more coverage parts with common elements.

71. A BOP eligibility focuses on relatively predictable small-business exposures.

72. A Coverage A is bodily injury and property damage liability.

73. B Coverage B covers listed personal and advertising injury offenses.

74. A Coverage C provides medical payments for eligible accidental injuries.

75. B Completed work falls within products-completed operations.

76. B Standard CGL uses a separate products-completed operations aggregate.

77. B Businesses in the alcohol trade need liquor liability; the CGL liquor exclusion applies.

78. A Part One pays benefits required by listed state workers compensation law.

79. A Part Two provides employers liability coverage.

80. B A factor above 1.00 generally increases premium.

81. A Classification rates commonly apply per $100 of payroll.

82. B Robbery involves force or threat against a person.

83. C Mysterious disappearance is unexplained and not automatically theft.

84. B The principal owes the obligation.

85. A The obligee receives the guarantee.

86. B A performance bond guarantees performance of the contract.

87. A The retroactive date limits how far back covered wrongful acts may occur.

88. B Employment Practices Liability addresses wrongful employment conduct.

89. B An SIR commonly applies to an umbrella-covered claim without underlying coverage.

90. B Domestic refers to the insurer state of formation.

91. B Another U.S. state makes it foreign in Texas.

92. C Formation under another country law makes it alien.

sections.title: Glossary
sections.html:
Glossary

Actual cash value. Replacement cost less depreciation under the common exam formula.

Adhesion. A contract drafted mainly by one party and accepted by the other, with ambiguity generally construed against the drafter.

Admitted insurer. An insurer holding a certificate of authority in the state.

Adverse selection. The tendency of higher-than-average risks to seek or retain insurance.

Aggregate limit. The most a policy pays for specified losses during a policy period.

Aleatory. A contract in which exchanged values may be unequal because performance depends on an uncertain event.

Appraisal. A process for resolving the amount of a property loss, not coverage.

Bailee. A person or business temporarily possessing property of another for a purpose.

Binder. Temporary evidence of insurance pending issuance of the policy.

Blanket insurance. One limit applying to multiple properties, types, or locations.

Bodily injury. Bodily harm, sickness, or disease, including resulting death as defined.

Burglary. Defined unlawful taking from premises involving signs of forcible entry or exit in traditional crime terminology.

Cancellation. Termination of a policy before its expiration date.

Certificate of authority. State authorization for an insurer to transact admitted insurance.

Certificate of insurance. Evidence summarizing coverage; it ordinarily does not amend the policy.

Coinsurance. A property provision requiring insurance to a stated percentage of value to avoid a loss penalty.

Combined single limit. One liability limit for covered bodily injury and property damage in an accident.

Concealment. Failure to disclose a material fact.

Consideration. The value exchanged by contracting parties.

Declarations. The policy section identifying insured, term, limits, property, forms, and premium.

Deductible. The part of a covered loss retained by the insured.

Domestic insurer. An insurer formed under the laws of the state in which it is being described.

Endorsement. A form that adds, deletes, or modifies policy provisions.

Excess insurance. Coverage providing limits above stated underlying insurance.

Exposure. A person, property, operation, or condition subject to loss.

Fidelity bond. Protection against specified dishonest acts, commonly employee dishonesty.

Foreign insurer. An insurer formed under another U.S. state or jurisdiction.

General damages. Compensatory damages for noneconomic harm such as pain and suffering.

Hazard. A condition increasing the frequency or severity of loss.

Indemnity. Restoration of an insured approximately to the preloss financial position.

Insurable interest. A lawful financial interest in the preservation of life or property.

Insuring agreement. The insurer basic coverage promise.

Liability. A legal obligation to another.

Limit. The maximum amount payable under a coverage, subject to policy terms.

Loss ratio. Incurred losses and loss adjustment expense compared with earned premium.

Market value. The price a willing buyer would pay a willing seller.

Moral hazard. Dishonesty or intent that increases loss probability.

Morale hazard. Carelessness or indifference because insurance exists.

Mortgagee. A lender holding a mortgage interest.

Mutual insurer. An insurer owned by policyholders.

Named peril. A cause of loss covered only when listed in the form.

Negligence. Failure to use reasonable care under the circumstances.

Nonadmitted insurer. An insurer without a state certificate of authority, which may write lawful surplus lines coverage if eligible.

Nonrenewal. Decision not to continue a policy for another term at expiration.

Occurrence. An accident, including continuous or repeated exposure to substantially the same harmful conditions, as defined.

Open peril. Direct physical loss covered unless excluded or limited.

Peril. The direct cause of loss.

Physical hazard. A tangible condition increasing the chance or severity of loss.

Premium. The price charged for insurance coverage.

Principal. The party whose obligation a surety guarantees.

Pro rata. Proportional allocation without a cancellation penalty.

Proof of loss. A formal insured statement supporting the facts and amount of a claim.

Property damage. Physical injury to tangible property or loss of its use as defined.

Proximate cause. The dominant cause setting an unbroken chain of events in motion.

Punitive damages. Damages intended to punish and deter especially wrongful conduct.

Rebating. Offering an unlawful inducement not specified in the policy.

Replacement cost. Cost to repair or replace with like kind and quality without depreciation.

Representation. A statement made as true to the best of the applicant knowledge.

Retention. Paying some or all of a loss rather than transferring it.

Risk. Uncertainty concerning loss.

Robbery. Taking property from a person through force or threat.

Salvage. Value remaining in damaged property.

Short rate. Cancellation calculation returning less than pro rata, creating a penalty.

Special damages. Measurable compensatory damages such as medical bills and lost wages.

Specific insurance. A separate limit applying to one item or location.

Split limits. Separate liability limits for bodily injury per person, bodily injury per accident, and property damage.

Stock insurer. An insurer owned by stockholders.

Subrogation. An insurer right after payment to recover from a responsible third party.

Surety. The party guaranteeing the principal performance to the obligee.

Umbrella. High-limit liability coverage that may be broader than scheduled underlying policies.

Underwriting. Selecting, classifying, and pricing risks.

Unilateral. A contract in which only one party makes an enforceable promise.

Vacant. Lacking occupants and sufficient contents for normal use under the applicable definition.

Vicarious liability. Liability imposed on one party for another conduct because of a relationship.

Warranty. A statement or promise guaranteed to be true.

Sources and Update Guide

The official outline is the controlling map for examination preparation. Before scheduling, check the outline effective date and compare any new topic or changed citation with this edition. The following primary sources support the examination structure and Texas sections.

Pearson VUE Texas Department of Insurance Licensing Exams. Exam scheduling page and official downloads, updated February 10, 2026. Open official source

Texas Insurance Code. Primary Texas statutory source; specific chapters are identified in the official outline. Open official source

Texas Administrative Code Title 28. Primary Texas insurance rules. Open official source

Texas Department of Insurance Consumer and Agent Resources. Official guidance on auto, home, workers compensation, and market mechanisms. Open official source

How to Update This Book

Check the Pearson VUE Texas insurance page for a newer content outline and candidate handbook.

Check TDI licensing pages for application fees, fingerprint procedures, agency financial responsibility, renewal, and continuing education.

Check the Texas Insurance Code and Administrative Code citations listed in the current state outline.

Review current TDI consumer pages for personal auto limits, PIP and UM or UIM requirements, cancellation, nonrenewal, FAIR Plan, TWIA, TAIPA, and workers compensation.

Change the edition date whenever a substantive rule, examination weight, fee, or procedure changes.
